newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's newcomer stocks are no flash in the pan.
newsitem.headline: Spain's newcomer stocks are no flash in the pan.

text.p: Investors have greedily gobbled up a handful of newcomers to Spain's stock market in recent months sending their shares sky high, but analysts say the new arrivals have even more to offer in the long term.

In the last year, Spain's issue-starved stock market has welcomed a mere three brand new retail offerings -- family-owned businesses Telepizza, Adolfo Dominguez and Sol Melia -- which have whipped up a flurry of interest.
In a market gripped by share fever, these three stocks have soared but remain at the top many analysts' buy recommendation lists.

"Aside from the fact that these stocks have benefited from the lack of offerings on the market, they are fundamentally good stocks that offer good growth prospects in the long term," said an analyst in Madrid.

Pizza delivery chain Telepizza has been a particular favourite among investors and its shares have almost tripled in value to 8,500 pesetas since its hugely successful launch last November which was 46 times oversubscribed.

Spain's leading hotel chain Sol Melia has also put in a good performance since it was launched last summer, jumping from an original placing price of 2,700 pesetas to 5,520 on Wednesday, and succeeded in joining the Ibex-35 index of leading shares in January.
Meanwhile, fashion house Adolfo Dominguez -- the most recent arrival -- broke records with its initial 70 percent public offer in March which was 112 times oversubscribed.
But despite this early burst of activity, analysts say these stocks have much to offer well into the long term.
Strong brand names, dominant market positions, good management and solid market growth potential combine to offer impressive profit growth prospects, analysts said.
Many analysts predict that profits at the three companies will grow by more than 20 percent to the year 2000.

"Telepizza has the strongest growth outlook in the medium to long term of all the companies listed on the Spanish stock market," Carlos Ramos, equity analyst at Ahorro Corporaccion Financiera (ACF) said.
Many analysts predict that Telepizza's profits will grow by a beefy 30 percent to the year 2000 while profits at Adolfo Dominguez and Sol Melia are forecast to grow nearer 20 percent.

"Sol Melia is one of the Spanish market's strongest growth stocks. We forecast compound profit growth of 20 percent at least to the year 2000 on the back of its expansion programme currently in progress," said Juan Correas, equity analyst at ACF in Madrid.
Strong brand names and leading positions in their markets are key to their attraction in the long term, analysts said.
Telepizza and Sol Melia are both leaders in their fields and are continually building market share while Adolfo Dominguez is among the best in Spain.
Telepizza has further strengthened its 52 percent share of the pizza market with the purchase of rival chain Pizza World.
Ambitious expansion programmes are also endearing the stocks to investors.
But some analysts said if they had any doubts about the companies it would lie in their expansion plans.
For example, Telepizza is now busy expanding in smaller towns and abroad having consolidated its position in the most important urban centres in Spain.
The fast food chain could be exposed to lower sales per store and higher risk, analysts said.
Adolfo Dominguez finds itself in the same boat.
The fashion group aims to dramatically expand its overseas presence which in 1996 accounted for 20 percent of sales.
Sol Melia is not so exposed to these risks as it only manages hotels, analysts said.
However Telepizza and Adolfo Dominguez appear to have planned ahead.
"By franchising new outlets they will cut down that risk and give us the good growth we expect," said an analyst at a Spanish bank in Madrid.
